claims.claim: EFNB2 expression levels are highest in mesenchymal and classical GBM subtypes in the TCGA dataset.
claims.source: In addition, analysis of 402 GBM from the TGCA dataset classified according to Verhaak et al. and corrected for IDH1 status, indicated that EFNB2 expression levels are highest in mesenchymal and classical GBM subtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c) (Verhaak et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: EFNB2 correlated with decreased survival in mesenchymal GBM.
claims.source: When tumours were divided into two groups on the basis of EFNB2 levels relative to median expression within subtypes, EFNB2 correlated with decreased survival in mesenchymal GBM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: In the absence of ephrin-B2, human GSC lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6c–h, we found that, similar to the murine GSC models, in the absence of ephrin-B2, GSC (but not SCR shRNA-transduced controls) lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2 and failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: In the absence of ephrin-B2, human GSC failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6c–h, we found that, similar to the murine GSC models, in the absence of ephrin-B2, GSC (but not SCR shRNA-transduced controls) lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2 and failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is supported by soft agar and cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6d,e.

claims.claim: EFNB2 knock-down cells gave rise to slower growing tumours in only 2 out of 10 animals, with the other 8 mice remaining tumour-free for >1 year.
claims.source: We found a dramatic impairment of tumour growth in the EFNB2 knock-down group relative to control, in that vector-transduced G26 formed GBM in all animals (as previously reported (Stricker et al., 2012) whilst EFNB2 knock-down cells gave rise to slower growing tumours in only 2 out of 10 animals, with the other 8 mice remaining tumour-free for >1 year.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data shown in Figure 7a-c.

claims.claim: Vascular contact was severely compromised in EFNB2 knock-down cells at 10 days following implantation.
claims.source: SCR GSC associated with the vasculature at this early time point (and at later stages of tumour growth), resulting in vascular co-option, as reported (Figure 7d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) (Watkins et al., 2014). In contrast, vascular contact was severely compromised in knock-down cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7d.

claims.claim: EFNB2 downregulation resulted in a marked decrease in proliferation, accompanied by an arrest in the G2/M phase of the cell-cycle in vivo.
claims.source: Furthermore, similar to GSC1Efnb2-/- murine cells, EFNB2 downregulation resulted in a marked decrease in proliferation, accompanied by an arrest in the G2/M phase of the cell-cycle, indicative of a cytokinesis block (Figure 7e,f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining and cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claims.claim: Ephrin-B2 drives tumour initiation by mediating vascular association and proliferation of human GSC.
claims.source: Thus, Ephrin-B2 drives tumour initiation by mediating vascular association and proliferation of human GSC.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo experiments with EFNB2 knock-down human GSC.

claims.claim: B11 strongly suppressed tumour growth in all animals without any evidence of toxicity, with three of six animals showing complete regression.
claims.source: Remarkably, B11 strongly suppressed tumour growth in all animals without any evidence of toxicity, with three of six animals showing complete regression, as judged by quantitative bioluminescence imaging, survival analysis and post-mortem examination of the injected brains (Figure 8a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo treatment data shown in Figure 8a-c.

claims.source: Analysis and quantification of the tumours immediately following treatment also revealed that, in contrast to vehicle-treated control tumours, invading tumour cells failed to associate with and coopt the vasculature (Figure 8d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8d.

claims.source: Furthermore, proliferation was reduced in B11 tumours relative to controls, with B11 samples containing many Ki67+ multinucleated cells, indicative of a cytokinesis defect (Figure 8e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 8e.

claims.source: Therefore, B11 suppresses G26 tumourigenicity through inhibition of ephrin-B2-dependent perivascular invasion and anchorage-independent proliferation, independent of angiogenesis.

claims.claim: Ephrin-B2 plays an important role in the pathogenesis of human GBM and its inhibition might be an effective strategy for curtailing GBM progression and recurrence.
claims.source: We conclude that Ephrin-B2 plays an important role in the pathogenesis of human GBM and its inhibition might be an effective strategy for curtailing GBM progression and recurrence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective findings with human GSC.

results.result: The authors generated two murine GSC models (GSC1 and GSC2) by sequentially introducing oncogenic lesions into normal neural stem cells. Both models retained stem cell properties in vitro, formed aggressive tumors in vivo with high penetrance, recapitulated human GBM histopathology and gene expression signatures (particularly mesenchymal subtype), and showed perivascular invasion patterns similar to human GBM.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C52 collectively demonstrate successful generation of relevant murine GBM models. The data includes comprehensive characterization: stem cell properties (neurosphere formation, differentiation), tumorigenic capacity (soft agar, in vivo tumor formation with specific penetrance and survival data), histopathological features (necrosis, neovascularization, marker expression), gene expression analysis (mesenchymal signature enrichment), and invasion patterns (perivascular migration, displacement of astrocyte endfeet). The models are validated through multiple independent assays with appropriate controls.

results.result: Using intravital imaging and in vitro migration assays, the authors demonstrate that GSC1 cells migrate along blood vessels while immortalized NSC (imNSC) remain stationary in groups. Selective deletion of endothelial ephrin-B2 enabled imNSC to migrate perivascularlly in vivo, demonstrating that vascular ephrin-B2 compartmentalizes non-tumorigenic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57, C61-C62 provide converging evidence from intravital imaging (Figure 1e,f) and in vitro assays (Figure 1g) showing differential migratory behavior. The genetic deletion experiment in endothelial-specific Efnb2 knockout mice (C61-C62) provides strong causal evidence that vascular ephrin-B2 is necessary for compartmentalization. Quantitative data on migration distances and boundary formation support the conclusions.

results.result: Recombinant ephrin-B2-Fc compartmentalized imNSC but not GSC in vitro, and knockdown of Efnb2 in endothelial cells disrupted boundary formation against imNSC, demonstrating that endothelial ephrin-B2 is both necessary and sufficient for compartmentalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 provide complementary gain-of-function (ephrin-B2-Fc) and loss-of-function (siRNA knockdown) evidence. The data from Figure 1i,j with Videos 3-4 demonstrate specificity of the ephrin-B2 effect. The conclusion that ephrin-B2 is necessary and sufficient is well-supported by these bidirectional experiments.

results.result: Elevated Ras signaling upregulates Efnb2 in GSC, and this upregulation is necessary and sufficient for GSC to evade ephrin-B2-mediated endothelial repulsion. Genetic deletion of Efnb2 in GSC1 restored boundary formation and blocked perivascular migration, while Efnb2 overexpression in imNSC enabled migration over endothelial cells and escape from vascular compartmentalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 establish the molecular mechanism through systematic gene expression analysis (qRT-PCR, Western blot), genetic manipulation (knockout and overexpression), and functional assays (migration assays in vitro and intravital imaging in vivo). The bidirectional genetic experiments (C66-C67) provide strong causal evidence. Changes in Eph receptor levels (EphB1, EphB2) were ruled out as the mechanism (C65), strengthening the conclusion that ephrin-B2 is the key mediator.

results.result: GSC overcome ephrin-B2-mediated repulsion through homotypic cell-cell interactions that depend on forward signaling. Approximately 20% of GSC are repelled on first contact with ephrin-B2, with repelled cells migrating as single cells or small groups while non-repelled cells migrate in larger groups. Disruption of cell-cell junctions blocked GSC migration over ephrin-B2, and expression of truncated ephrin-B2 lacking reverse signaling (ΔCEfnb2) was sufficient to enable migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 dissect the mechanism through quantitative analysis of cell behavior (Figure 3a,b), disruption of cell-cell contacts (low Ca2+, DN-N-cadherin), and structure-function analysis (ΔCEfnb2 construct). The data demonstrate that forward signaling between neighboring GSC cells, rather than reverse signaling, mediates escape from repulsion. The experiments are well-controlled and the logic is sound.

results.result: GSC exhibit constitutively high levels of activated Eph receptors (p-Eph) due to elevated ephrin-B2 expression, leading to desensitization to exogenous ephrin-B2 stimulation. This constitutive activation can be mimicked by ephrin-B2 overexpression in imNSC and is dependent on endogenous ephrin-B2. Pretreatment of imNSC with ephrin-B2-Fc enabled migration over ephrin-B2 boundaries, confirming that Eph forward signaling activation is the mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 provide comprehensive mechanistic evidence through Western blot analysis of p-Eph levels (Figure 3e,f), genetic manipulation (ephrin-B2 overexpression and deletion), disruption of cell-cell contacts, and functional rescue experiments (ephrin-B2-Fc pretreatment). The data show that constitutive Eph activation desensitizes cells to exogenous stimulation, and this is confirmed by in vivo immunofluorescence (C83). The mechanism is well-established through multiple converging lines of evidence.

results.result: Ephrin-B2 is sufficient to transform immortalized NSC and necessary for GSC tumorigenicity in vivo. Efnb2 overexpression in imNSC1 resulted in tumor formation with similar kinetics to GSC1 (median survival 28 days), while Efnb2 deletion in GSC1 strongly suppressed tumor growth (7/9 animals developed slower-growing tumors, 2/9 remained tumor-free).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 demonstrate the transforming capacity of ephrin-B2 through in vivo tumorigenic studies with bioluminescence imaging and survival analysis (Figure 4a,b). The bidirectional genetic experiments show that ephrin-B2 is both necessary (deletion suppresses tumors) and sufficient (overexpression induces tumors) for transformation. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5-10) and the effects are dramatic and statistically significant.

results.result: Ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent proliferation through reverse signaling, independent of homotypic cell-cell contact. ImNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 formed large colonies in soft agar at similar efficiency, while imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 (lacking reverse signaling) did not form colonies, and disruption of cell-cell junctions did not affect colony formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 establish the mechanism of ephrin-B2-mediated proliferation through soft agar assays with structure-function analysis (ΔCEfnb2) and disruption of cell-cell contacts (DN-N-cadherin). The data clearly distinguish the reverse signaling-dependent, contact-independent mechanism of proliferation from the forward signaling-dependent, contact-dependent mechanism of invasion. The experiments are well-controlled and the conclusions are logical.

results.result: Ephrin-B2 reverse signaling enables cells to bypass an anchorage checkpoint at G2/M. In suspension culture, imNSC arrested with 4n DNA content (G2/M arrest), while GSC1 continued to proliferate. This arrest could be rescued by ephrin-B2 overexpression (full-length but not ΔC) and was reinstated by Efnb2 deletion in GSC. Cell cycle profiles in vivo matched those in methylcellulose culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 demonstrate the cell cycle mechanism through FACS analysis of PI-stained cells in attachment vs. suspension culture (Figure 4e,f). The structure-function analysis (full-length vs. ΔC ephrin-B2) confirms reverse signaling is required. The in vivo validation (C102-C103) strengthens the physiological relevance. The data are quantitative and reproducible across multiple cell lines (GSC1, GSC2).

results.result: Ephrin-B2 reverse signaling drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis. Methylcellulose cultures lacking ephrin-B2 reverse signaling (imNSC1, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2, GSC1 Efnb2-/-) contained a much larger proportion of EdU-negative binucleated cells compared to adherent conditions, indicative of cytokinesis block, while cells with intact ephrin-B2 reverse signaling had similar low percentages of binucleated cells in both conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 identify the specific cell cycle defect through EdU pulse-labeling and phalloidin staining to distinguish cycling from arrested binucleated cells (Figure 5a,b). The use of EdU to distinguish G2/M arrest from cytokinesis failure is appropriate. The data are quantitative and consistent across multiple genotypes, supporting the conclusion that ephrin-B2 specifically enables cytokinesis in suspension.

results.result: Ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis through RhoA-mediated reverse signaling. Levels of active RhoA were low in suspended cells lacking ephrin-B2 reverse signaling but greatly increased in cells expressing high levels of full-length ephrin-B2. Constitutively active RhoA (V14) rescued the cell cycle arrest of imNSC1 and GSC1 Efnb2-/-, while dominant-negative RhoA (N19) arrested imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 in G2/M.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 establish RhoA as the downstream effector through RhoA pull-down assays (Figure 5c) and genetic rescue experiments with constitutively active and dominant-negative RhoA mutants (Figure 5d). The bidirectional genetic manipulation provides strong causal evidence. The data are quantitative and the effects are specific to cells in suspension, supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: In human GBM patient specimens, ephrin-B2 is expressed in 25-90% of tumor cells and co-localizes with the stem cell marker ALDH1 in perivascular neoplastic cells at the infiltrative tumor margin, indicating expression in stem-like cells invading along blood vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 provide immunohistochemical evidence from 8 patient tumors (Figure 6a, Table 3). The co-expression analysis with ALDH1, a validated GSC marker, supports the conclusion that ephrin-B2 is expressed in the GSC compartment. The analysis focused on the infiltrative margin, which is most relevant for invasion. The data are descriptive but appropriate for establishing clinical relevance.

results.result: In primary human GSC lines and TCGA data, EFNB2 expression correlates with mesenchymal gene expression and is highest in mesenchymal and classical GBM subtypes. EFNB2 correlated with decreased survival specifically in mesenchymal GBM.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 provide bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data from 8 GSC lines (Figure 6b) and TCGA data from 402 GBM patients (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d). The correlation analysis is appropriate and the survival analysis is stratified by subtype. The data support the clinical relevance of ephrin-B2, particularly in mesenchymal GBM, though the survival correlation is only significant in one subtype.

results.result: EFNB2 knockdown in human GSC (G26, G166, G19) abolished their ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2 and to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in G2/M cell cycle arrest, recapitulating the findings from murine GSC models.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 validate the key findings in human GSC through shRNA-mediated knockdown and functional assays (migration, soft agar, cell cycle analysis) shown in Figure 6c-e. The effects are consistent across three independent human GSC lines, strengthening the generalizability. The data directly parallel the murine findings, supporting translational relevance.

results.result: EFNB2 knockdown in human G26 GSC dramatically impaired tumor growth in vivo, with only 2/10 animals developing slower-growing tumors while 8/10 remained tumor-free for >1 year. At 10 days post-implantation, EFNB2 knockdown cells showed severely compromised vascular contact and marked decrease in proliferation with G2/M arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 demonstrate the therapeutic potential through in vivo tumorigenic studies with adequate sample sizes (n=10) and long follow-up (>1 year). The mechanistic analysis at early timepoints (10 days) links the tumor suppression to impaired vascular association and proliferation defects (Figure 7d-f). The effects are dramatic and statistically significant, supporting the conclusion that ephrin-B2 drives tumor initiation in human GSC.

results.result: Treatment of established G26 tumors with ephrin-B2-blocking antibody B11 strongly suppressed tumor growth in all animals without toxicity, with 3/6 animals showing complete regression. B11-treated tumors showed failure of vascular association, reduced proliferation, and multinucleated cells indicative of cytokinesis defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 demonstrate therapeutic efficacy through treatment of pre-established tumors with bioluminescence monitoring, survival analysis, and mechanistic studies (Figure 8a-e). The treatment was initiated after tumors formed but before angiogenesis, allowing assessment of direct effects on tumor cells. The complete regression in 50% of animals is remarkable. The mechanistic data (vascular association, proliferation, cytokinesis) link the therapeutic effect to the proposed mechanisms. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-6).

results.result: The introduction establishes the clinical and biological context for GBM research, including disease characteristics, current treatment limitations, GSC properties, invasion routes, and the rationale for studying GSC-vascular interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C11-C32 provide background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to establish the scientific context. These are well-established facts in the GBM field and are appropriately referenced. The claims set up the rationale for the study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

results.result: The authors describe their experimental approach and provide background on the Eph/ephrin system, including its roles in cell behavior and cancer, and previous links between specific Eph/ephrin family members and GBM.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 describe the study design (C33) and provide background on Eph/ephrin biology (C34-C36) and prior GBM research (C37-C38), all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the scientific foundation but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: The authors summarize their main findings: endothelial ephrin-B2 inhibits non-tumorigenic cell migration; GSC override this through ephrin-B2 upregulation and constitutive Eph forward signaling; ephrin-B2 reverse signaling promotes anchorage-independent proliferation via RhoA; ephrin-B2 overexpression transforms imNSC; and ephrin-B2 is expressed in perivascular GSC in human tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are summary statements of the main findings that are supported by the detailed experimental data described in other claim groups. These represent accurate summaries of the work but are redundant with the detailed results.

results.result: The authors conclude that targeting ephrin-B2 may be an effective strategy for simultaneous inhibition of invasion and proliferation in GBM and that ephrin-B2 plays an important role in human GBM pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C128 are concluding statements that are well-supported by the collective experimental data, particularly the therapeutic studies with EFNB2 knockdown and B11 antibody treatment. However, these are interpretive conclusions rather than direct experimental findings. The use of "may be" and "might be" appropriately indicates these are proposed therapeutic strategies requiring further validation.
